items.reason: Source: "in their succourless empty-handedness" — succourless means without succor (no aid, no support ships). The candidate's "helpless" suggests incapacity, the opposite of the heroic point. "javelin-throwing islands" for "javelin islands" is an acceptable brief gloss (see open question).
items.new: I freely assert that the cosmopolitan philosopher cannot, for the life of him, point to one single peaceful influence that, within the last sixty years, has worked more powerfully upon the whole broad world, taken all together, than the high and mighty business of whaling. One way and another, it has produced events so remarkable in themselves, and so continuously momentous in their consequences, that whaling may well be regarded as that Egyptian mother who bore offspring that were themselves pregnant from her womb. It would be a hopeless, endless task to catalogue all these things. Let a handful be enough. For many years past the whale ship has been the pioneer in ferreting out the remotest and least known parts of the earth. She has explored seas and archipelagoes that had no chart, where no Cook or Vancouver had ever sailed. If American and European warships now ride peacefully in once savage harbors, let them fire salutes to the honor and glory of the whale ship, which first showed them the way and first interpreted between them and the savages. They may celebrate as they like the heroes of Exploring Expeditions, your Cooks, your Krusensterns; but I say that scores of anonymous captains have sailed out of Nantucket who were as great as your Cook and your Krusenstern, and greater. For in their unaided, empty-handed state, in heathenish, shark-filled waters and by the beaches of unrecorded, javelin-throwing islands, they battled with virgin wonders and terrors that Cook, with all his marines and muskets, would not willingly have dared. All that is made such a flourish of in the old South Sea Voyages was only the lifelong commonplace of our heroic Nantucketers. Often, adventures to which Vancouver devotes three chapters, these men thought unworthy of being set down in the ship's ordinary log. Ah, the world! Oh, the world!

items.reason: Source: "took down the words from Other, the Norwegian whale-hunter of those times" — "Other" is correctly kept as printed (decision 7), but in "the words of Other" a modern reader will take "Other" as the common word ("the Other"). Add the minimal gloss "a man named", as the edition already does for "one Bulkington" at 23.0; the printed name is unchanged.
items.new: The whale no famous author, and whaling no famous chronicler? Who wrote the first account of our Leviathan? Who but mighty Job! And who composed the first narrative of a whaling voyage? Who but no less a prince than Alfred the Great, who with his own royal pen took down the words of a man named Other, the Norwegian whale hunter of those times! And who delivered our glowing eulogy in Parliament? Who but Edmund Burke!

items.new: And as for me, if by any possibility there is some as yet undiscovered prime quality in me; if I ever deserve any real reputation in that small but lofty, hushed world to which I might not unreasonably aspire; if hereafter I do anything that, on the whole, a man would rather have done than have left undone; if, when I die, my executors — or more accurately, my creditors — find any precious manuscripts in my desk, then here and now I ascribe all the honor and the glory to whaling in advance; for a whale ship was my Yale College and my Harvard.

items.new: Stubb was the second mate. He was a native of Cape Cod, and so, according to local usage, was called a Cape-Cod-man. A happy-go-lucky type; neither cowardly nor valiant; taking dangers as they came with an indifferent air; and in the most urgent crisis of the chase, toiling away, calm and collected as a journeyman joiner hired for the year. Good-humored, easy, and carefree, he presided over his whale-boat as if the deadliest encounter were only a dinner, and his crew all invited guests. He was as particular about the comfortable arrangement of his part of the boat as an old stagecoach driver is about the snugness of his seat. When close to the whale, in the very death-lock of the fight, he handled his pitiless lance coolly and offhandedly, as a whistling tinker handles his hammer. He would hum his old rigadig tunes while flank to flank with the most furious monster. Long habit had, for this Stubb, turned the jaws of death into an easy chair. What he thought of death itself, there is no telling. Whether he ever thought of it at all might be a question; but if he ever did happen to turn his mind that way after a comfortable dinner, no doubt, like a good sailor, he took it to be a sort of call of the watch to tumble aloft and bestir themselves there, about something he would find out when he obeyed the order, and not sooner.

items.new: I was struck by the singular posture he maintained. On each side of the Pequod's quarter-deck, and pretty close to the mizzen shrouds, an auger hole had been bored about half an inch or so into the plank. His bone leg was steadied in that hole. One arm raised, holding onto a shroud, Captain Ahab stood erect, staring straight out beyond the ship's ever-pitching bow. There was an infinity of the firmest fortitude, a determined, unsurrendering willfulness, in the fixed and fearless, forward dedication of that gaze. He spoke not a word, nor did his officers say anything to him. Yet by their every small gesture and expression, they clearly showed the uneasy, if not painful, awareness of being under a troubled master's eye. And more than that — moody, stricken Ahab stood before them with a crucifixion in his face, with all the nameless, regal, overpowering dignity of some mighty grief.

items.new: Before long, after his first appearance on deck, he withdrew to his cabin. But after that morning, he was visible to the crew every day — either standing in his pivot-hole, or sitting on an ivory stool he had, or walking heavily across the deck. As the sky grew less gloomy and even began to turn mild, he became less and less of a recluse, as if, when the ship first sailed from home, nothing but the dead winter bleakness of the sea had kept him shut away. Gradually, he was almost constantly in the open air. But for all he said or visibly did on the now sunny deck, he seemed as unnecessary there as an extra mast. The Pequod was only making a passage, not actively cruising. Nearly all the whaling preparations that needed overseeing the mates were fully capable of handling. So there was little or nothing outside of himself to occupy or excite Ahab now, and so to chase away, for that one interval, the clouds that were piled layer upon layer on his brow — just as all clouds always choose the loftiest peaks to pile themselves upon.

items.reason: Source: "the longer linked with life, the less man has to do with aught that looks like death" (i.e. old men sleep little). "the less he wants anything to do with" adds a motive the source does not state.
items.new: Old age is always wakeful, as if the longer a man is linked with life, the less he has to do with anything that looks like death. Among sea captains, the old graybeards are the ones who most often leave their beds to visit the night-wrapped deck. So it was with Ahab, except that lately he seemed to live so much in the open air that, truly speaking, his visits were more to the cabin than from it. "It feels like going down into one's tomb," he would mutter to himself, "for an old captain like me to be descending this narrow hatch to my grave-dug bed."

items.reason: Source: "Am I a cannon-ball, Stubb, that thou wouldst wad me that fashion?" — "wad" is the cannon-loading term (wadding), which makes the joke; "pad" loses it.
items.new: "Am I a cannonball, Stubb," said Ahab, "that you'd wad me like that? But go your way — I forgot. Down to your nightly grave, where the likes of you sleep wrapped in shrouds, getting used to the one you'll fill at last. Down, dog, and to your kennel!"

items.new: "What do you think of that now, Flask? Isn't there a small drop of something queer about that, eh? A white whale — did you catch that, man? Look here — there's something special in the wind. Be ready for it, Flask. Ahab has something bloody on his mind. But shh — he's coming this way."
